name: Renuka
definition: Renuka is a composite portrait of a Scheduled Caste woman working in Gangavathi's groundnut and oilseed processing economy, navigating daily wage insecurity, school costs for three children, and the gap between Article 371(J) promises and lived opportunity in Koppal district. She represents the tension between canal-irrigated prosperity along the Tungabhadra Left Bank and the Scheduled Caste households who process the harvest but rarely own the land.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Renuka works the sorting and bagging line at a small groundnut oil mill on the Gangavathi-Munirabad road, six days a week when the mill runs at full capacity during the November-to-March crushing season. She earns two hundred and twenty rupees for an eight-hour shift, though the owner sometimes stretches the day to ten hours without extra pay when a large farmer's lorry arrives. In the lean months she takes daily-wage work weeding sunflower fields or loading onion sacks at the APMC yard, earning one-eighty to two hundred rupees a day. Her husband drives a rented auto-rickshaw on the Gangavathi town routes; on a good day he clears three hundred rupees after fuel and the daily rental of one-fifty to the owner. The household's joint income sits around twelve to fourteen thousand rupees a month during the oil-crushing season, dropping to eight or nine thousand in the summer lean months. They have no savings account with any real balance; every rupee is allocated before it arrives. Renuka leaves home at seven in the morning, returns by six, then cooks, helps her eldest daughter with schoolwork, and falls asleep by ten.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Renuka lives with her husband, their three children—a daughter in Class 10 at the government high school in Gangavathi town, a son in Class 7 at the same school, and a younger daughter in Class 3 at the primary school in their colony—and her mother-in-law, who is in her late sixties and can no longer work. The household rents a one-room asbestos-roofed house with a shared tap and toilet in a Scheduled Caste colony on the edge of Gangavathi, paying twelve hundred rupees a month. Renuka was married at sixteen, shortly after she stopped school in Class 8; her own schooling ended because her parents needed her to work and saw no future return in keeping a daughter in school. She hopes her eldest daughter will finish SSLC and perhaps study further, though the cost and the pressure to marry her off early weigh on every conversation. Her husband's income is unpredictable, and his drinking on some evenings cuts into the week's budget. Renuka manages all the household money, plans every meal around the cheapest dal and vegetables, and absorbs the blame when there is not enough. Her mother-in-law helps with the younger children when Renuka is at work, but her health is declining and she needs medicines the household struggles to afford.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Renuka's own schooling ended in Class 8 when her parents, both agricultural labourers, could not see the point of continuing and needed her to work. She can read Kannada slowly and write her name and basic lists, but she regrets not finishing school and is determined that her children, especially her daughters, will study further. Her eldest daughter attends the government high school in Gangavathi town, a four-kilometre ride on the KKRTC bus each day; the Shakti free-travel scheme has made that possible, saving the family about six hundred rupees a month in bus fare. The school charges no tuition, but Renuka spends around fifteen hundred rupees a term on books, uniforms, and exam fees. Her daughter is a steady student, ranking in the top half of her class, and dreams of becoming a teacher. Renuka has heard about the Article 371(J) reservation for college seats and government jobs, and the family hopes that quota will give her a chance. The youngest daughter attends the colony primary school, where the mid-day meal is often the best meal of her day. Renuka herself cannot help with homework beyond Class 5 level, so her eldest daughter tutors the younger two. The cost of private tuition, which many better-off families use, is completely out of reach.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Renuka suffers from chronic lower-back pain, a legacy of years standing on the mill floor and bending to load sacks, but she has never taken a full day off for it because she cannot afford to lose the wage. She has an Ayushman Bharat card, but the nearest empanelled hospital is in Hosapete, over thirty kilometres away, and the cost and time of traveling there for anything less than an emergency feels impossible. For fever, stomach pain, or her back, she goes to a private clinic in Gangavathi where the doctor charges one-fifty for a consultation and writes a prescription she fills at the pharmacy next door, usually spending another two to three hundred rupees. Her mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure; the government hospital in Gangavathi gives her medicines some months but not others, and when the stock runs out Renuka has to buy them at full price, which can cost six hundred rupees. Her eldest daughter had severe anaemia two years ago, diagnosed at a free school health camp; the anganwadi worker insisted Renuka get iron tablets, but sustaining the treatment and improving her diet proved difficult. Renuka herself has not had a full health check-up in years. She worries about her husband's drinking and the toll it takes on his liver and their household peace, but talking about it only leads to fights. The 108 ambulance service is known in the colony, but people say it is slow to arrive and sometimes does not come at all.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Renuka is Madiga, part of Gangavathi's substantial Scheduled Caste population working in the oilseed economy, construction labour and sanitation work. Her colony is exclusively Scheduled Caste, spatially separated from the main town and the dominant-caste neighborhoods; the colony has a shared water tap, irregular electricity, and a small Ambedkar statue at the entrance that the community gathers around on Ambedkar Jayanti every year. Renuka's family worships both Ambedkar and the village deity, and she visits the Anjaneya temple on the edge of town for her children's health and exam success. She is not deeply religious, but she observes the festivals—Ugadi, Diwali, Ambedkar Jayanti—and fasts occasionally for her children's well-being. The anganwadi worker in the colony is a helpful presence, running the feeding programme and connecting families to government schemes, though Renuka finds the paperwork for most schemes overwhelming. Caste shapes every dimension of her life: where she lives, the kind of work she can get, the way upper-caste people speak to her in the market, and her daughter's experience in a mixed-caste classroom. Renuka has heard about Basavanna and the Sharana movement's rejection of caste, taught as local pride in school textbooks, but she sees little of that equality in daily life.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Renuka has a ration card, an Ayushman Bharat card, and her children's Aadhaar cards, but navigating the welfare system feels like a continuous maze of incomplete information and lost paperwork. The family receives subsidized rice and kerosene through the PDS, though the shop sometimes runs out or opens late. She has heard about the Kalyana Karnataka Region Development Board and Article 371(J) funds, but she has no sense of what that money has actually built in Gangavathi beyond a few school buildings and a hostel she has never seen inside. The local anganwadi worker helps her understand some schemes, but most government programmes feel designed for people who already know the system and have time to visit offices repeatedly. Renuka's husband once tried to get a loan under a self-employment scheme to buy his own auto, but the paperwork and the need for a guarantor defeated him. She respects the local MLA because he is seen in the town, but she has never met him or attended a party meeting. Renuka does not follow state politics closely, but she listens when neighbors talk about reservation quotas, job recruitment, and whether Scheduled Caste families are actually getting the promised share. She feels that the government talks about Kalyana Karnataka being special and backward, but the daily experience is just wage work, school fees, and waiting.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Renuka's deepest worry is her eldest daughter's future: whether she will finish SSLC with good marks, whether the family can afford to send her to college in Gangavathi or Hosapete, whether the Article 371(J) reservation will actually open a government job or college seat for a Scheduled Caste girl from a labour household, and whether they can hold off marriage pressure from relatives long enough for her to study. She is proud that her daughter is the first in the family to reach high school and determined that she will not repeat Renuka's own truncated schooling. She worries about money every single day—the rent, the monthly school costs, the medicines, the price of onions and dal, and what will happen when her mother-in-law needs serious medical care they cannot afford. She resents the way upper-caste people in Gangavathi still treat her and her family, the spatial segregation of the colony, and the gap between the Constitution's promise of equality and the reality of her daughter being made to sit separately in one classroom incident she will never forget. She blames the oil mill owner for underpaying workers, her husband for drinking, and the government for announcing schemes that never seem to reach her household in full. Renuka demands better: a permanent job with a real salary, her daughter's education funded properly, a hospital in Gangavathi that actually works, and respect in public spaces. She sees Gangavathi's irrigated wealth and wonders why her family, working in the heart of the groundnut economy, lives in a rented asbestos room with no savings and no security.
